title: How the Printing Press Changed the World
paragraphs: Prior to the mid-fifteenth century, the reproduction of texts in Europe depended entirely on the scribe’s hand. Copying a single manuscript could absorb months of labour, and each transcription introduced fresh errors, so that no two copies of a work were ever quite identical. Books were accordingly scarce, costly and largely confined to monasteries, universities and the households of the powerful.

Johannes Gutenberg’s achievement in Mainz lay less in any single breakthrough than in the synthesis of several: type cast from a durable alloy in reusable moulds, an oil-based ink capable of adhering to metal, and a screw press borrowed from the vintner’s trade. Together these allowed pages to be composed from interchangeable letters, printed in quantity and dismantled for the next job, turning the book from a unique artefact into a reproducible commodity.

The diffusion of the technology was astonishingly rapid. The Bible completed in his workshop around 1455 proved that mechanical reproduction need not compromise quality, and by the close of the century presses were active in hundreds of towns across the continent, collectively issuing millions of volumes. The economics of knowledge had been upended almost overnight.

Its repercussions were profound and far-reaching. Affordable print nurtured a literate public, while cheap pamphlets enabled figures such as Martin Luther to circumvent traditional gatekeepers and address readers en masse. Standardised editions, moreover, allowed scholars to scrutinise, correct and extend one another’s findings with a precision hitherto impossible, which is why historians frequently cite the press as a precondition for the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and the public sphere itself.
